title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
primary_topics: Chapter 6 covers Art's two-year junior-associate period (1961-1963) at Dean Jovito R. Salonga's law firm -- the aborted Yale dream (scholarship awarded, Fulbright/Smith-Mundt travel grant denied because of his student-activist record), Salonga's offer as consolation ('I will thus teach you what I learned from the University of the Philippines, Yale and Harvard'), and the firm itself as a powerhouse of future national leaders: Sedfrey A. Ordonez (Cory's Secretary of Justice in 1987), Pedro L. Yap (Chief Justice of the Supreme Court 1988), Neptali Gonzales (Senate President 1992-93, 1995-96, 1998), and Salonga himself (Senate President 1987-1992).

Salonga as the third and most enduring mentor of CJP's life: surrogate father after Temi's 1955 death, Cosmopolitan Church layman who 'did not smoke or drink or gamble,' lived 'simple, almost ascetic life,' Harvard MA + Yale JSD (rare combination), instilling 'integrity, prudence, fairness and temperance' as the life-defining virtues. The chapter quotes extensively from Art's March 14, 2016 eulogy for Salonga, including the 'things that money cannot buy' formulation.

Two formative courtroom encounters with national-rank lawyers, both of which Art lost but learned more from than from cases he won: (1) Atty. Jose W. Diokno ('Father of Human Rights Advocacy in the Philippines,' 1944 bar topnotcher, Secretary of Justice 1962, Senator 1963) at the Court of First Instance under Judge Angel H. Mojica (Art's former professor) -- Salonga sick at the last minute, Art unprepared facing the legendary Diokno, who chose to move for postponement *himself* out of 'graciousness and humility' to a young, nervous lawyer; and (2) the standing Salonga warning when contending against Atty. Claudio Teehankee ('You better prepare our trial brief very well because we are going to be up against one of the best lawyers in town').

Claudio Teehankee as the hero-worshipped libertarian model: Ateneo de Manila prep summa (1938), LL.B summa (1940) and bar topnotcher that same year, future 16th Chief Justice; described by Art as 'a social engineer who saw the law as an instrument to build a just society' who 'reached for the stars to render justice via the all-encompassing rule of law,' standing for liberty 'even at the cost of his personal safety and that of his family.' Teehankee becomes the doctrinal lineage source of CJP's later libertarian jurisprudence.

The 'four hallmarks' formulation distilled from these mentors -- Independence, Integrity, Industry, and Intelligence -- that the chapter positions as the personal-character architecture Art would later carry to the Bench. The chapter argues that CJP's later judicial identity was not abstract policy but a synthesis of named lineages: Salonga's incorruptibility, Diokno's fairness-even-against-self-interest, Teehankee's libertarian courage.

stances.claim: Dean Salonga's offer was not merely a job substitute for the lost Yale plane fare -- it was educationally equivalent or superior: 'Through him, I had the best of four educational worlds: FEU, UP, Harvard and Yale.' The chapter argues that the consolation became the actual gift, with Yale-style policy orientation transmitted via apprenticeship rather than degree.

Salonga is the role model of CJP's adult life -- not merely a competent boss but the source of CJP's professional ethics architecture (integrity, prudence, fairness, temperance) and substantive jurisprudential orientation ('law as a brick in building the social structure'). The 2016 eulogy is the chapter's central documentary evidence.
stances.rhetorical_move: lineage thesis explicitly stated; 'things money cannot buy' as the doctrinal capsule

stances.claim: Diokno's gallant postponement -- choosing to forgo a sure victory against an unprepared junior -- is presented as the highest form of professional ethics: not merely competence but fairness that costs you. The chapter implicitly argues that this incident shaped CJP's later judicial habit of giving even losing parties their full day in court.
stances.rhetorical_move: ethical-asymmetry illustration; courtroom courtesy as substantive justice

stances.claim: Teehankee as the libertarian source: the social-engineer-rather-than-technician conception of law, the rule-of-law commitment 'at the cost of personal safety,' the 'reaching for the stars to render justice' is the lineage of CJP's later libertarian-philosophy framework that he would crystallize as Chief Justice. The chapter is explicit that Teehankee was 'hero-worshipped.'
stances.rhetorical_move: ideological-lineage claim; CJP's libertarianism not invented but inherited

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 covers Art's two-year junior-associate period at Dean Jovito R. Salonga's law firm (1961-1963), opening with the upward turn -- cum laude graduation, #6 bar finish, April 1961 marriage to Leni -- and the aborted Yale dream. Salonga had recommended Art for a Yale Law School scholarship (board, lodging, and tuition awarded), but the Fulbright/Smith-Mundt travel grant from the US Embassy was denied because of Art's activist record as student leader. 'A crushing blow,' the chapter calls it -- financial-disadvantage helplessness striking again. Salonga's consolation offer became the actual gift: 'I will thus teach you what I learned from the University of the Philippines, Yale and Harvard.' Art joined Salonga, Ordoñez, Sicat and Associates as junior associate and worked alongside the future leadership of the Republic -- Sedfrey A. Ordonez (Cory's Secretary of Justice in 1987), Pedro L. Yap (Chief Justice of the Supreme Court 1988), Neptali A. Gonzales (Senate President 1992-93, 1995-96, 1998), and Salonga himself (Senate President 1987-1992). Salonga's Harvard MA + Yale JSD -- a combination the two rival ivies normally did not permit -- let him distinguish for Art the case-method orientation of Harvard from the policy-oriented approach of Yale (a lawyer who 'should go beyond' rules and doctrines and 'do what would serve the interests of the nation and the world community'); Art reports gaining 'the best of four educational worlds: FEU, UP, Harvard and Yale.' Beyond legal technique, Salonga gave Art a character architecture: integrity, prudence, fairness, temperance -- the 'life-moving virtues' -- and an ethic of life in which the Cosmopolitan Church layman 'did not smoke or drink or gamble,' lived 'simple, almost ascetic,' indifferent to titles and honors. The chapter quotes extensively from Art's March 14, 2016 eulogy, including the distilled capsule about 'the things that money cannot buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity, and a reverential regard and love for God.' Two courtroom encounters give the chapter its narrative spine. In the first, Salonga fell ill at dawn and telephoned Art to cover a Court of First Instance hearing under Judge Angel H. Mojica (Art's former FEU Law professor) -- against the legendary Atty. Jose W. Diokno, 'Father of Human Rights Advocacy in the Philippines,' 1944 bar topnotcher (the war had interrupted his studies, and the Supreme Court had granted him qualifying-test permission), Secretary of Justice in 1962, Senator in 1963. Salonga had given his word there would be no postponement, so Art appeared alone and unprepared. Diokno, observing the young *compañero*, then did the unexpected: 'in fairness to my young *compañero* and knowing that Atty. Salonga would not tell a lie about his health, I myself am now moving to postpone the hearing.' Art was stunned, relieved, grateful -- Diokno 'now loomed even higher in his esteem,' the chapter recording the lesson: 'He did not belittle me but instead gave me respect.' The second encounter is structural rather than singular: every time Salonga faced Atty. Claudio Teehankee (Ateneo summa 1938 prep, summa 1940 LL.B, 1940 bar topnotcher, future 16th Chief Justice) he would warn his junior, 'You better prepare our trial brief very well because we are going to be up against one of the best lawyers in town.' Art hero-worshipped Teehankee -- 'a social engineer who saw the law as an instrument to build a just society,' who 'reached for the stars to render justice via the all-encompassing rule of law,' stood for liberty 'at the cost of his personal safety and that of his family,' and pioneered the libertarian philosophy in the Philippines. The chapter concludes with a distilled synthesis of these three lineages: 'Independence, integrity, industry and intelligence would become the hallmarks of his judicial career' -- not Art's invention but Salonga's incorruptibility, Diokno's fairness-even-against-self-interest, and Teehankee's libertarian courage combined into the personal-character architecture that CJP would carry to the Bench.
